name: LM317
seoDesc: LM317: work out resistor (R2) from the resistor and the output voltage. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The LM317 calculator turns the resistor and the output voltage into resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 2)))))). It suits whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the LM317 calculator work?
sections.html:
The LM317 calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 2)))))) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 1)))))) and the output voltage.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the LM317 calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 2))))))=(1 ÷ 5) × resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 1)))))) × (4 × output voltage − 5)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 1)))))) = 10 Ω and Output voltage = 10 V. The calculator returns Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 2)))))) = 70 Ω.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 2)))))) = 70 Ω should be roughly the size you expected from Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (Resistor (r 1)))))) = 10 Ω and Output voltage = 10 V.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in ohms, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Voltage, opening in volts

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The LM317 calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the resistor and the output voltage — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the LM317 calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — resistor for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the LM317 calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns resistor (R2), derived from the resistor and the output voltage. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the LM317 calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the resistor and the output voltage, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter resistor (R1) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Resistor (r 1) opens in ohms and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Resistor (r 2) = 70 Ω. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the LM317 calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
